title: Distributed Transaction Challenges
description: Understand the fundamental challenges of managing transactions across microservices.

data.text: Distributed transactions are one of the hardest problems in microservices. Amazon, Netflix, and Uber all faced challenges maintaining data consistency when operations span multiple services. Traditional ACID transactions do not work across service boundaries.

In a monolith, a single database provides ACID guarantees. In microservices, each service has its own database. A distributed transaction spanning multiple services requires coordination across network boundaries, which introduces latency, partial failures, and complexity.

data.title: Distributed Transaction Challenges
items: No atomic commit across services: Each service commits independently
Partial failures: One service may succeed while another fails
Network latency: Coordination adds significant latency
Blocking: Two-phase commit blocks resources during prepare phase
Scalability: Distributed locks and coordination limit throughput

data.title: CAP Theorem Again
data.text: Distributed transactions require strong consistency (C) and partition tolerance (P), sacrificing availability (A) during network partitions. This is why most distributed systems choose AP over CP.

data.title: Example: E-commerce Order Transaction
data.code: An order requires updating Inventory, Payment, and Shipping services. If Payment succeeds but Inventory fails, the system is inconsistent.

data.caption: Distributed transaction flow
data.definition:
graph LR
    O[Order Service] -->|1. Call| I[Inventory Service]
    O -->|2. Call| P[Payment Service]
    O -->|3. Call| S[Shipping Service]
    I -->|Success| O
    P -->|Success| O
    S -->|FAILS| O
    O -->|INCONSISTENT STATE| DB[(Database)]

items.question: Can I use two-phase commit in microservices?
items.answer: Two-phase commit is possible but rarely recommended. It blocks resources, reduces availability, and is complex to implement correctly. Use Saga pattern instead.

items.question: What is the alternative to distributed transactions?
items.answer: Use the Saga pattern with compensating transactions. Each service commits independently; if a step fails, compensating actions undo previous steps.

items.question: How do Amazon and Netflix handle this?
items.answer: Amazon and Netflix use eventual consistency and Saga patterns. They accept temporary inconsistency and reconcile differences through background jobs.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Distributed transactions are hard and should be avoided
ACID guarantees do not extend across service boundaries
Saga pattern with compensating transactions is the standard solution
Embrace eventual consistency in distributed systems
data.takeaway: Design for eventual consistency; avoid distributed transactions whenever possible.
